chapter: Black and Tan and Kansas City nightlife
title: Bootleg half-pints from his mother's flat and the monthly printer
summary: With friends he sold bootleg whiskey from the empty flats his mother managed, and recalls a printer who came each month on a bender.

story.theme_name: Gangsters, bootleggers and rough clubs of Prohibition
story.community_name: Gangsters, bootleggers and the Prohibition-era clubs

blocks.x: I got so I'd go out on Twelfth Street. We used to have...we moved up to another flat when Momma was the manager of it, and we had a...always kept maybe one or two apartments empty. So, we got so a bunch of us fellows got together, and we had a...a joint. We sold whiskey. Bootleg whiskey. We sell it by the half-pint. And this flat that my mother had--she was the manager--and when she'd tell me to show somebody the apartment, I show them everybody's apartment but that one. We had two rooms up front, three rooms in the back. We had the three rooms in the back where we worked at, and we had two rooms up in the front.

Used to have a white fellow used to hang around with us. He was a printer...worked in a newspaper. He show up every month. When he get on his benders, he come by, sittin' around: "All you poor boys need a haircut!"
"We all ain't been doin' so good."

So we all go to the barber and get a haircut, and he would buy a half-pint for hisself and buy a half-pint for the boys. He didn't give nobody none out of the half-pint he had. He drank that all t'...by hisself. He turned it up and just drank it--one drink. He'd drink the whole half-pint. He'd do that three...four times, then he'd get him a bottle to put in his pocket. He used to stay maybe four...five...maybe ten days on his bender and then when he got ready to go back to work, when his money run out, he would get it on tab 'cause know he's comin' back. He get it on tab. So cats used to think he was drunk, you know, and he didn't remember but he go in the bathroom and mark it on the wall how many half-pints he'd got. So, we used to tease him all the time. I don't remember his name either. He was somethin' else.

So the cat...when he come back next month to pay off, the cats say, "You owe us thirty dollars." Say, "No, no, no, no, no, no, no, no, no. I don't owe you no thirty dollars. Owe you twenty-one dollars." Say, "Whaddya mean? I sold you so many half-pints..." "Jus' a minute." He go in the bathroom, and "Shit, look, I mark 'em down." And couldn't get by that. "I mark 'em down...how many half-pints I got."

One time he got drunk...we looked for him for two days. He went in the basement...went down in the basement where they kept the coal at...was down there asleep. So I had to go down in the basement one day and find him down there asleep...set layin' on the floor asleep. So I got him up, took him upstairs, washed his face and everything, got him back straight. He went right back to drinkin'. I never will forget him. He used to be a good, little white fellow. He come by a-a-a-a-a-l-lll... every month. He didn't miss a month. He come by there every month. And he'd be off. I don't know where he's off but just took off. He was a helluva printer, workin' at a...some newspaper. And when he come, didn't know...we'd know what time he gettin' ready to come...the end o' the month, look for him. We sittin' on the...cats be sittin' on the step waitin' on him. There we get a lot of free drinks when he show up. Time for him to show up, here he comes, walkin' down the street...get off...get offa the streetcar ...come walkin' down the street. Here he come. He had a dance he done. He used to do a dance...jump all over the pla...look like he was doin' the Charleston...knock over all the chairs an' everything, doin' his dance. Do your dance, Cous. He would dance. He would get in there and knock over
all the chairs an' everything but he never spilt that half-pint. He hold onto that. He have that right in his pocket. He'd do his dance and he get up and take him a big drink out of his bottle.
